query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, adding chromium (Cr) enhances oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective Cr-rich oxide scale that impedes further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high-entropy alloy lacking sufficient anti-oxidant alloying elements, characterized by poor or moderate oxidation resistance at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Increase the Cr content in the alloy composition (compared to the baseline) while keeping other alloying elements constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidative environments (e.g., air exposure at temperatures around 800–1000 °C) where protective oxide layer formation is critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer (likely Cr2O3) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: When exposed to high-temperature oxidizing conditions, the added Cr oxidizes preferentially to form a continuous Cr2O3 layer that acts as a barrier, reducing the ingress of oxygen and slowing further oxidation of the underlying material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with increased Cr content will show a significantly lower oxidation rate (measured as reduced mass gain, thinner oxide scale, or improved oxide scale integrity) compared to the baseline alloy with lower Cr content.
generation.baseline: The original alloy composition with little or no extra Cr addition, resulting in inferior oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected within the studied temperature range; extreme environments or interactions with other alloying elements might modify the protective effect. The precise Cr content for optimal protection is not determined and may vary with the alloy system.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between Cr content and oxidation resistance (e.g., exact critical Cr level, scale thickness, and long-term stability of the oxide film) remains uncertain and likely depends on other alloying additions and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the baseline Cr content and another with an elevated Cr content. Subject both sample sets to controlled high-temperature oxidation tests in air (e.g., at 900 °C for a fixed duration) under identical thermal cycling conditions.
measurements: Measure mass gain over time as an indicator of oxidation rate.
Characterize the oxide scale's thickness and composition using SEM, XPS, or TEM.
Assess the integrity and adhesion of the oxide layer via surface analysis techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with increased Cr content do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (mass gain, oxide thickness, or scale integrity) compared to the baseline alloys under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that added Cr improves oxidation resistance via forming a protective oxide layer is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The alloy is rich in Ni, Co, Fe with a mixing entropy of the alloy to 1.60 R, which can be categorized as a high entropy alloy [14] . The term of mixing entropy is calculated by: ΔS mix = −R(X A lnX A + X B lnX B + …), where R is the gas constant, X A means the molar fraction of constituent A in whole alloy, X B means the molar fraction of constituent B, and so on. Al, Ti and Nb are the γ′ forming elements for precipitation strengthening. Cr is added to provide oxidation and corrosion resistance. The slight carbon content is for grain-boundary pinning purpose, and minor amounts of Mo and W are added for solid-solution strengthening. The design of HESA was also assisted by CALPHAD-based simulation (JMatPro [55] , Ni-alloys database), and the aim is to contain more than 60 vol% of strengthening L1 2 γ′ as commercial Ni-based superalloys.
